state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a toy car on a track and you want to move it 3 units to the left. Would you move the car up or down to achieve this? Think about how this relates to shifting the graph of \(y=f(x)\) to \(y=f(x-3)\).

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if I'm moving the car left, I wouldn't move it up or down at all - I'd just move it sideways. So does that mean f(x-3) moves the graph to the left instead of up? But I'm still confused about why it's left and not right, because there's a minus sign...

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a basketball hoop in your backyard. If you move the hoop 3 feet to the left, would the ball need to go up or down to make a basket? Think about how this relates to shifting the graph of \(y=f(x)\) to \(y=f(x-3)\) and why it moves to the left instead of the right.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it now - if the hoop moves left, the ball stays in the same place, so it would still go up into the hoop the same way. So the graph moves left, not up. But I'm still confused about why the minus sign makes it go left instead of right - like, shouldn't minus mean it goes the opposite way?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that don't directly address why the student thinks the transformation is vertical rather than horizontal, and while the student progresses from thinking it's vertical to recognizing it's horizontal, they remain confused about the direction (left vs right) throughout, suggesting the core misconception about the minus sign isn't resolved.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (toy car, basketball hoop), these analogies fail to illuminate the core mathematical concept of why f(x-3) shifts right rather than left, and the teacher doesn't ground the counterintuitive minus-sign behavior in experiential understanding.
